Summary: During the seven days of Tabernacles, the appointed burnt offerings are brought each day, decreasing in number through the week, with a sin offering daily.
Commandment: Offer the appointed offerings of the Feast of Tabernacles each day of the feast.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.
Function: During the seven days of Tabernacles, the appointed burnt offerings were brought each day, decreasing in number through the week, with a sin offering daily — a ceremonial law of festival abundance. Its goal was to keep the feast of booths supplied with offerings all week, the decreasing numbers marking the days as they passed. It did not address a particular evil; its work was worship and rejoicing, not restraint. The offerings dwindled as the week went on, and the feast ended as it had begun: at the altar.
